results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book describes two DIY approaches to chroma keying — an HSV color-curve method and a 3D RGB color-cube method — and then warns that building your own is probably more hassle than it's worth [S2].

**Method 1: HSV to color curves** ([S1][S17])
Roll your own chroma keyer the same way you'd make your own luma keyer (Section 2.1.3): start with an operation that converts the RGB image to HSV, then pipe the HSV image into a color curve. In the resulting curves, the RED curve now holds Hue data, the GREEN curve holds Saturation, and the BLUE curve holds Value (brightness), so you adjust the three curves to include or exclude the Hue, Saturation, and Value ranges of the target object [S1][S17].

**Method 2: A 3D color keyer** ([S7][S8])
This is a "flexible variation" based on the exact color of the item of interest rather than luminance — essentially a grossly simplified version of Primatte's operating principles, where backing pixels (e.g., green screen) are plotted in the RGB color cube [S7]. The recipe: take R1G1B1 as the normalized value (0–1) of the center point — the color you want to isolate — and R2G2B2 as the normalized value of each pixel, and enter the resulting equation in a math node or expression format [S8]. The book even offers the test image `greenscreen.tiff` to try it on, plus the color target image `Chroma key target.tif` for practicing keys on various parts of a picture [S5][S8]. One caveat: the retrieved text references "this equation" without actually showing its formula, so the exact expression is missing from what I have.

**How the classical version works, for context** ([S13])
Internally, a chroma keyer converts RGB to HSV or HSL, sets a starting pixel value as the "center" of the key, then defines separate Hue, Saturation, and Value ranges — pixels inside go to 100% white, outside go to black, and tolerances on each setting soften the edge [S13]. The homemade curve version is just a manual implementation of that same idea.

**The book's verdict — and what counts as a "keyer"**
Unlike the DIY luma keyer, where a clever build can genuinely outperform the basic version, the homemade chroma keyer "will probably be more hassle than its worth" — worth trying once to test your mettle, but an off-the-shelf keyer is hard to improve on [S2]. There's also a terminology point: strictly, a chroma keyer is one that converts RGB to HSV/HSL and keys on chrominance and luminance; most greenscreen tools (Keylight, Ultimatte) are actually color-difference keyers, with Primatte the notable true 3D chroma keyer [S4]. All the DIY approaches in the book are software/node-based — no hardware or circuit-based chroma keyer is described in the evidence.

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
**The short version:** a nonsquare pixel is a pixel whose width and height are unequal, quantified by its **pixel aspect ratio**; the book treats it as both a display concept and a practical post-production concern that emerges with anamorphic cinema and SD video.

## What a nonsquare pixel is

A nonsquare pixel is "a pixel whose width is not the same size as its height" — its shape is rectangular rather than square, and the width-to-height relationship is expressed as the **pixel aspect ratio** (pixel width ÷ pixel height) [S2][S3][S10]. That ratio is independent of the image's overall aspect ratio, which is a common point of confusion [S10][S13]. On a properly adjusted computer monitor, pixels are square with a pixel aspect ratio of 1:1; the "nonsquare" label refers to the shape of the pixel in the final display format, not to the pixels on the monitor you're working on [S1][S2]. A system that handles nonsquare-pixel material simply applies a temporary geometric transformation for display — the underlying image data is never modified [S4].

## Where nonsquare pixels show up in cinema

Format | Pixel characteristics | Pixel aspect ratio
--- | --- | ---
Computer monitors, HD, graphics software | Square | 1:1 [S1][S9]
SD video (NTSC-DV 720×480, PAL-DV 720×576) | Rectangular | e.g., 10:11 for NTSC [S9][S13]
Anamorphic/"squeezed" film (e.g., Cinemascope) | Optically distorted | 2:1 squeeze in Cinemascope [S5][S7]

Film formats that optically distort an image are called **squeezed** or **anamorphic** formats — "anamorphic" comes from the art world and literally describes a distorted image that can be restored to its original shape [S7]. The book uses Cinemascope, the most common anamorphic format, because its 2:1 squeeze most dramatically illustrates the concepts [S5].

## Why it matters in film production and post

- **SD video is the everyday case:** NTSC-DV and PAL-DV use rectangular pixels, while HD, graphics software, and computer monitors use square pixels — so footage crossing between these worlds needs handling [S9].
- **Output compensation is usually required:** with NTSC's pixel aspect ratio of 10:11 (pixels slightly taller than wide), a perfectly round circle created in the computer would appear as an ellipse on an SD monitor unless scaled; whether you scale manually or the system automates it depends on your setup [S13]. The problem arises whenever your output medium displays images differently than your intermediate compositing system does [S16].
- **Rotating squeezed footage is the classic trap:** rotating a squeezed element without accounting for the squeeze produces distortion. The correct procedure is to unsqueeze, rotate, and then resqueeze along the x-axis. Even a small 5° rotation shows visible error on a round subject, so the advice is to "double-check everything if you are working with nonsquare pixels" so such problems don't sneak into the final result [S8].

```
Squeezed frame ──► display-time unsqueeze (data unchanged) [S4]

Safe rotation workflow:
unsqueeze ──► rotate ──► resqueeze along x-axis [S8]
```

In short, the book's core message: nonsquare pixels are a property of the *display* format, not the pixel data itself — but failing to account for them during compositing, rotation, and delivery to SD video will visibly distort your images [S4][S8][S13].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The corpus gathers these as short working maxims scattered across the drawing chapters — the throughline is: draw for **clarity, boldness, and life**, and save special effects for when they're actually needed.

### Clarity & legibility
- You should be able to **blacken in your drawings and still read what is happening**; keep decoration inside the main outline, and make the outlines themselves interesting [S1][S22].
- Draw **one idea per sketch**, and draw attention to one idea at a time, "just like when speaking" [S3][S7].
- **Have something to say in your image — don't doodle** [S3].
- If part of a drawing doesn't work, **cut it out and rework it**; don't be afraid to redraw in search of the best solution [S3].

### Boldness & media
- **Draw BOLD** — grease pencil, marker, or 2B pencil, never a hard pencil — so drawings read from across the room, and **number your drawings** [S2].
- Draw bold and expressive generally; the important idea of the sketch should be highlighted and **all else subordinated to it** [S6].

### Composition & design
- **Avoid symmetry** — it's boring and makes drawings look cut out; use angles and dynamic asymmetry instead [S6].
- **Play straight lines against curves** for interest, and draw borders so you have to compose to them [S3][S6].
- Don't get too clever with tricky camera angles — that just makes the drawing ambiguous [S6].

### Life & expression
- **Show how the character feels** — feel the pose and the emotion kinetically in your own body; a person is always "doing" something, so express the purpose [S6].
- **Darken pupils when drawing eyes** [S3].
- Use **straight-line symbols for stretches, bent lines for squashes**, and watch body landmarks where bones reach the surface, like hipbones and ribs [S6].
- The same pose can carry a "long idea" — a force that sweeps through the body, e.g. from one leg through the back and down to the wrist — so look for the application of force across the whole figure [S8].

### Process & technique
- Learning to draw has **two parts: technique** (perspective, anatomy, force, shape) **and honest observation** — combining them lets you diagnose your own work, e.g. "is the drawing generic? Look more. Is it specific but flat and dead? Use technique." [S5][S19].
- **Rough sketch first** — the rough is about "grasping the appearance/state of what you will draw," and it varies per person from near-final to a maze only the artist can pen in [S9].
- **Drawing multiple moments of the same subject** is more telling than a single drawing — a great exercise for proportion, volume, and personality [S10][S25].
- **Drybrush (speed lines) and motion blur** illustrate the optical blur the eye sees when an object moves too fast to see clearly [S21]; use drybrush very sparingly, and only when drawings are so widely spaced the eye struggles to connect them — well-planned spacing makes it unnecessary [S4].
- One aside mentions drawing in **chiaroscuro** ("...or the line that never existed anyway") — the lines of an average illustration don't exist in life [S13][S23].
- Related material also notes **contrapposto poses** to express movement and momentum, and the facial-action-coding subtlety that in AU 18 vs. 35, cheek-sucking (35) makes the lips smaller and protruding [S28][S11][S14].

Two tips stand out as the most repeated: **clarity wins over cleverness** (silhouette legibility, one idea per sketch) and **boldness beats neatness** (heavy media, expressive poses) — nearly every other tip serves one of those two.

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The book draws the line at the viewing environment: **transcoding handles displays that differ only in colorimetry, while color rerendering handles displays that differ in white levels, contrast, or viewing conditions** [S1][S2].

**Transcoding** applies when the two displays have identical black levels, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma, but different primary chromaticities. In that case the encoded colors are transcoded by 1) linearizing the first display's encoded RGB values, 2) converting them to CIE XYZ values, 3) converting those CIE XYZ values to the corresponding RGB values for the second display, and 4) reimposing the encoding nonlinearity [S2]. Because the viewing environment is unchanged, it is a straightforward colorimetric conversion.

**Color rendering**, by contrast, is "the transformation of an image to account for differences in viewing environment" [S4]. When contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar between the two displays, the best solution is **color rerendering**: any color rendering implicitly or explicitly done for the first display is undone, and the non-color-rendered CIE XYZ values are then color rendered for the second display [S1].

| | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| **When used** | Displays match in black level, white luminance, viewing conditions, gamma; primaries differ | Contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar |
| **What differs** | Primary chromaticities only (colorimetric) | Viewing environment (appearance) |
| **Process** | Linearize RGB → CIE XYZ → second display's RGB → reimpose encoding | Undo first display's rendering → non-color-rendered CIE XYZ → render for second display |

A few workflow distinctions the book emphasizes:

- **Color rendering normally happens before encoding**, prior to the quantization and rounding specified by the color space encoding. The book's example: a still camera producing JPEGs color-renders the captured image to account for the difference between a subject in bright desert sunlight and the reproduction on an office monitor whose peak white luminance is hundreds of times less powerful [S4].
- **Undoability matters.** With raw encodings, color rendering can be done downstream before the finished shot is shown, but it is hard to undo if the camera manufacturer baked color rendering into a non-raw format [S6]. That is exactly why the rerendering recipe begins by undoing the first display's rendering — it only works cleanly when that rendering can be reversed [S1].
- The same idea shows up in the ACES pipeline: the RRT provides the color appearance rendering for a dark-surround theatrical viewing environment, and each display gets its own Output Device Transform to render the RRT data correctly for that device [S3][S9].

The book indexes the full discussion under the section heading "Transcoding versus Color Rerendering" (p. 613) [S13][S23].

results.question: What does the book say about FACE OFF?
results.answer:
In the corpus, **"face-off" appears as a cinematic stunt term, not as a discussion of the John Woo film.** Three senses show up, and the first is the book-defined one:

- **Stunt term (defined in the film-production glossary):** a *face-off* is a fall that starts **face-first**, but where the performer **tucks and rotates at the last minute to land on their back** [S1]. It sits alongside other cinematography/stunt vocabulary like *eye line*, *fast lens*, *diffusion*, and *digital* [S1][S18].
- **Fight-choreography sense:** fighters "square off and face each other in fighting stances," and "Fighter A meets Fighter B in the center of the ring" [S7][S9]. The fight-choreography book dedicates a chapter (p. 174) to basic fighting terminology by category [S16], and notes the coach/corner man's concern for not getting a fighter hurt [S24].
- **Not the same thing:** the F-M FACS book's *"The Face of Code"* [S2][S6] is a facial-coding platform, unrelated to the physical "face-off" concept.

**Key limitation:** the corpus contains no analysis of the 1997 film *Face/Off* (John Woo) — if that's what you meant, it isn't covered in the retrieved material.

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
**The core idea: movement is never defined in isolation — it only exists as a relationship between the object and its background (or the frame line).** ["the book" here covers several related sources in the corpus, synthesized together]

## The definitional core
- **Relative movement** is the basis: movement of one object is gauged by its changing position relative to a second, stationary object — e.g., a black circle appears to move because its position changes relative to a stationary green circle and the frame [S1][S22].
- In the screen world, visual movement can be produced **only** when an object moves in relation to the frame line; if it doesn't, there is no movement [S3][S13]. This is why an object can move in a limited number of directions on screen — the screen is only two-dimensional [S13].
- **Induced movement** is the reverse case: a moving object transfers its movement to a nearby stationary object, so the stationary object appears to move while the moving one appears still [S4].
- Every moving object generates a **track** (actual or virtual), and movement is categorized by direction, quality, scale, and speed [S14]. The greatest contrast to object movement is no movement at all — **tableau staging**, where object movement is minimized in favor of stationary arrangement [S7].

## Handling the object-with-background relationship
When the camera moves, the background has to cooperate — and when it can't be shot that way, compositing steps in:

- **Match moving:** when the foreground camera moves, the background must move appropriately. Unless foreground and/or background can be photographed with a motion-control camera, tracking data must be extracted from the foreground image and applied to the background during compositing [S5][S19].
- **Tracking motion:** tracking analyzes the motion of an object in a shot and creates a motion path from it; other clips or elements can then be attached to follow that same path [S20]. In Fusion, clips have no inherent position/rotation/scale, so a transform node must be added and attached to the tracker [S23]. A planet background following the foreground shot's camera movement is given as exactly this kind of use [S8].
- **Z-depth limits:** Z-depth information is generally unavailable for live-action elements, so Z-compositing is typically useful only for combining CG elements; and partially transparent objects make per-pixel depth assignment impossible — the new element would be placed behind the foreground object while the foreground still reveals the original background behind it [S12].
- **Motion blur extraction:** a motion-blurred object over a reasonably neutral background is fairly easy to extract with a blurred rotoshape; over a detailed background it becomes much harder, because any soft-edged matte that includes the blur area also pulls in background detail [S9].

## Examples from the screen world
- **Shot #1:** an object's movement (a moving car, a running actor) begins in Q7 (lower left) and moves in a straight line to Q9 (lower right); **Shot #2** has curved movement starting where Shot #1 ended [S2].
- **Shots #3 and #4** superimposed reveal two completely separate lines or tracks generated by the moving objects — the contrast of continuum of movement [S6].
- A two-shot edit: a wide shot of an actor standing in a doorway followed by a close-up of the same actor, showing how **continuum of movement** matters across cuts [S17].
- **Lens + camera interaction:** a telephoto's reduced field of view, combined with a circular tracking move around a static subject, makes the background appear to revolve quickly behind them [S16].
- Even statics obey physics: an object or character has weight and moves only when a force is applied — Newton's first law [S18].

**Takeaway:** the sources treat the background not as a passive backdrop but as the reference system that makes movement legible — and once the camera moves, the background must be manufactured to match, via match moving, tracking, and composite paths.

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
## Core idea

Across the film-editing texts in your corpus, **sound editing is the postproduction phase where the finished soundtrack is assembled — and it is treated as at least as demanding as picture editing**. The 35th chapter of one editing textbook ("The Sound Edit and Clarity") and David Sonnenschein's *Sound Design* both argue that a wrong sound decision can undermine visuals almost instantly, and that without an effective soundtrack, the visuals will not succeed [S1].

## What the sound edit is

- Sound details are worked out in the **editing phase**: anything production didn't capture in original sound is created in postproduction [S1].
- Because of the sheer number of tracks, the sound edit is **more elaborate and requires many more decisions than the picture edit** [S1].
- The editor (or dedicated sound designers and editors) gathers additional audio files that **augment or replace production-recorded audio**, often generating a new, more realistic-sounding "reality" for the narrative [S4].
- The assembled soundtrack typically layers **dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley sounds**, overseen by a sound designer whose creative input is compared to the director of photography's role for the picture [S12, S18].
- Related elements named in the sources include ambient sound and walla, offscreen effects, spot effects, wild sound, sound-effects libraries, room tone/presence tracks, and sound logs [S7].

## Goals: narrative clarity and believability

The editor's first task is determining the **narrative point of the scene**, which sound must support and surround [S1]. The rough sound edit has the same goal as the rough picture assembly: believability of performance and a progressive sense of story, with dramatic emphasis and metaphor reserved for the fine cut [S8]. Believability is called the **most urgent task** — because sound is processed more rapidly by viewers than visuals, unconvincing sound undermines the picture and loses audience involvement [S9].

## Techniques and process

- Editing choices depend on production type, genre, content, purpose, sound-asset quality, and how the piece will be presented; but special care in **building and mixing tracks** applies everywhere, from a two-track music video to a blockbuster with 62 or more tracks [S10].
- The sound editor can try **manipulating speed and pitch**, and prepares an overall design that is transmitted to the director as a guide for the rerecording mix [S2, S3, S5].
- Practical tools named include pitch shifting, time compression, reverb, equalization, and hum removal, while timecode keeps picture and sound in sync [S15, S31].
- Historically, the sources note that early sync problems (disk recording and Movietone) made dialogue scenes nearly uneditable, restricting editing to silent sequences until rerecording and multiple cameras became common [S13].

## The author's argument

The texts share one core claim: **sound carries the picture, not the other way around.** Auditory stimuli affect audiences on physiological, psychological, and emotional levels, which is why even "silent" films were never meant to be silent — music was arranged for screenings from the start [S11, S16]. High-quality sound is therefore essential to visual storytelling [S27], and skilled sound design can break through the 2-D image to create a 3-D spatial experience [S29].

## Examples

- **The Battle of Algiers (1966)** — authenticity of the soundtrack is central to the audience's involvement in this recreation of Algeria's independence struggle [S1].
- **Creative foley substitutions** — cheese grating and wet pillow sounds for a punch, crumpled cellophane for fire, salt sprinkled on paper for rain, rice for hail, and hands on soggy newspaper for walking in mud, building on Jack Foley's pioneering work and musique concrète [S29, S32].

One caveat: none of the retrieved passages offers a single formal definition sentence of "sound editing"; the picture above is assembled from the chapter discussions and index material in the sources.

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
**The book's central radio-writing rule is blunt: write sparely, unless the concept genuinely demands a lot of words and fast action.** Sparse writing lets the voice talent read slowly, quietly, one word at a time [S2][S16].

## What "spare" means

- **Minimal copy, maximal silence.** Bare-bones execution "leaps out of the radio," and silence is to radio what white space is to print — it enlarges the idea it surrounds [S10].
- **A concrete word budget:** if a 60-second spot is a house, a :30 is a tent — "a different animal," roughly 60 words [S21]. (For context, spots typically run 10–60 seconds, with longer "brokered time" formats as an exception [S14].)
- **The goal is underwriting:** "Overwriting is the most common mistake people make in radio. Be a genius. Underwrite." [S3]

## Why the book insists on it

- Spare copy gives the voice talent room to slow down and create quiet, deliberate moments [S2][S16].
- Most radio spots are promotional, and clients often tack promotional tags onto the end that eat into the total time — sparse writing leaves room for them [S1].
- A fat script forces you to edit under studio pressure without client approval, which the book calls the worst outcome [S4].
- Radio only works with frequency, so a clean spot that can repeat well matters more than one stuffed with words [S11].

## Techniques for staying sparse

- **Mandatories first:** write and time the required material (e.g., a bank's legal ending) as sparely as possible; whatever time is left over is where your commercial has to fit [S3].
- **Don't draft full scripts while brainstorming** — scribble the general concept on a Post-it Note instead [S5].
- **Attack the brief one spot at a time.** Spots written to one strategy and one thought add up to one brand, even if their structures and sounds differ [S8].

## Examples in the book

- **The two unexpected ideas:** radios as pieces of furniture versus a radio in your pocket — Sony's Masaru Ibuka set the "pocketable" goal precisely because it was unexpected, challenging engineers to pursue the technology until it was small enough to be useful [S9][S12][S13].
- **A spare script line** for the beer-as-foreign-aid idea: "American-made Red, White and Blue beer. Red, White and Blue is less expensive than planes or computers." [S17]
- **"Walking on the moon"** as a bare-bones concept: "It's a long way up. The air is thin." [S9][S20]

The through-line: a radio spot exists only while it's playing [S8], and radio draws on the listener's imagination [S19] — so the words you leave out are what make the idea bigger.
